lessons.title: Brahman, Atman and the Hindu Gods

before.content_html:
Brahman — The Universal Soul

Hinduism is one of the world’s oldest living religious traditions. At its heart is the concept of Brahman: the ultimate reality, the universal soul, the single divine power that underlies everything that exists. The Chandogya Upanishad (3:14.1) describes Brahman as all of this universe and teaches that the entire cosmos arose from Brahman, lives within Brahman, and will return to Brahman. Brahman is infinite, without beginning or end, beyond complete human description.

One important dimension of Brahman is that Hindus speak of Brahman as both one and many. Brahman is the single ultimate reality, yet Brahman is also present in all things — in every person, every creature, every aspect of the natural world. The Katha Upanishad (5:2) teaches that Brahman, the inner self, dwells within the hearts of all living beings. A classic analogy in Hindu teaching is salt dissolved in water: the salt cannot be seen, but it is everywhere in the water. In the same way, Brahman permeates all existence while remaining beyond full perception.

Key Fact

Brahman is the ultimate reality and the source of all life (Chandogya Upanishad 3:14.1). Brahman pervades all things (Katha Upanishad 5:2). A helpful analogy: salt dissolved in water is everywhere yet invisible — just as Brahman permeates the universe.

Atman — The Individual Soul

Atman is the individual soul or true self within each living being. The Bhagavad Gita, one of Hinduism’s most important scriptures, teaches extensively about the nature of atman. At Bhagavad Gita 2:12, the god Krishna explains to the warrior Arjuna that there was never a time when either of them did not exist, and there will never be a time when they cease to exist. This establishes the eternal nature of the individual soul.

Bhagavad Gita 2:17 states that the soul is indestructible: the body may be slain, but the soul that pervades the body cannot be destroyed. This verse is one of the most frequently cited passages in GCSE Religious Studies because it clearly distinguishes the body (mortal, changing) from the atman (immortal, unchanging). The relationship between Brahman and atman is debated within Hinduism: the Advaita Vedanta school (associated with the philosopher Shankara) teaches that atman and Brahman are ultimately one and the same — the individual soul is not separate from the universal soul. This is summarised in the Sanskrit phrase Tat Tvam Asi (‘Thou art that’).

Hindu theology expresses the different functions of Brahman through a range of deities. The Trimurti is the three-fold form of the divine, representing the three great cosmic functions. The Kurma Purana (1:6, 1:9, 1:26) is one of the scriptural sources for this concept.

Brahma is the creator deity — responsible for bringing the universe into existence at the start of each cosmic cycle. Despite his cosmic importance, Brahma has relatively few dedicated temples in modern Hinduism, partly because creation is seen as completed.

Vishnu is the preserver — responsible for maintaining and sustaining the universe. Vishnu is central to the Vaishnavism tradition, one of the largest traditions within Hinduism. Vishnu is believed to descend to earth in physical form as an avatar whenever the balance of good and evil is threatened.

Shiva is the destroyer — but destruction in Hindu thought is not simply negative. Shiva destroys the old to make way for renewal and transformation. Shiva is central to the Shaivism tradition. The diversity between Vaishnavism and Shaivism illustrates the rich variety within Hinduism — the tradition is not monolithic but encompasses many different theological emphases.

Avatars — Krishna and Rama

The concept of the avatar is central to the Vaishnavism tradition. An avatar is a descent of a deity into the physical world in a particular form. The Bhagavad Gita (4:5–8) contains a passage in which Krishna explains to Arjuna that he takes birth in the world in age after age: whenever righteousness declines and unrighteousness rises, he manifests himself. This doctrine means that Vishnu’s avatars are not arbitrary but purposeful — appearing when the world is in moral crisis.

Krishna is one of the most beloved deities in all of Hinduism. He appears in the Bhagavad Gita as Arjuna’s charioteer, but reveals himself as a manifestation of Vishnu. Krishna is associated with divine love, playfulness and spiritual wisdom. His teachings to Arjuna on the battlefield form the core content of the Bhagavad Gita — arguably Hinduism’s most widely read scripture worldwide.

Rama is another of Vishnu’s principal avatars. His story is told in the epic poem the Ramayana. Rama is portrayed as the ideal king, husband and son — an embodiment of dharma (righteous duty). His battle to rescue his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana, aided by the monkey general Hanuman, is celebrated during the festival of Diwali.

Beyond the Trimurti and Vishnu’s avatars, two deities are especially important in popular Hindu devotion. Ganesh is the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati. He is the remover of obstacles and the lord of beginnings, and is invoked at the start of new ventures, journeys and religious ceremonies. His elephant head is often explained through a story in which Shiva, unaware Ganesh was his son, severed his head, and then replaced it with the first head available — that of an elephant.

Hanuman is the monkey deity who plays a crucial role in the Ramayana epic as the devoted servant of Rama. He is associated with strength, devotion (bhakti) and selfless service. Hanuman’s complete dedication to Rama makes him a model of devotional worship for many Hindus.

Key Fact

The Trimurti: Brahma (creator), Vishnu (preserver), Shiva (destroyer/transformer). Vishnu’s avatars include Krishna (divine teacher and lover) and Rama (ideal king and embodiment of dharma). The Bhagavad Gita 2:17 teaches that the atman (individual soul) is indestructible and cannot be killed even when the body dies.

practice_questions.text: Give two names used for God in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: Brahman; Brahma; Vishnu; Shiva; Krishna; Rama; Ganesh; Hanuman; Atman (as divine within).

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'atman' in Hinduism?
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for: the individual soul or true self within each living being, believed to be eternal and indestructible. One mark for a partial answer: 'the soul' or 'the self'.

practice_questions.text: Describe Hindu beliefs about the nature of Brahman.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description covering Brahman as ultimate reality and universal soul, source of all life (Chandogya Upanishad 3:14.1), present in all things (Katha Upanishad 5:2), the salt-in-water analogy, and the relationship with atman. Includes explanation of why this matters (all life has divine value). Secure: Clear description of Brahman as ultimate reality, with reference to sacred text and the one-and-many nature. Developing: Basic description of Brahman as 'God' or 'the universal soul' without development. Emerging: Simple statement that Brahman is God.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the concept of avatar influences the way Vaishnavas practise their faith.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains what an avatar is (Vishnu's descent to earth in physical form), cites Bhagavad Gita 4:5-8 (Krishna appears when righteousness declines), identifies key avatars (Krishna, Rama), explains influence: devotion to Krishna through bhakti and Hare Krishna chant; celebrating festivals such as Diwali (Rama's return); reading the Bhagavad Gita as Krishna's direct teaching; pilgrimage to sites associated with Krishna. Secure: Clear explanation of avatar concept with two developed examples of influence. Developing: Basic explanation of avatars; limited influence points. Emerging: Names Krishna or Rama without connecting to the avatar concept.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Hindu beliefs about the relationship between Brahman and atman.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Belief 1: Brahman pervades all living beings including the individual atman — the Katha Upanishad (5:2) teaches Brahman dwells within the hearts of all. Belief 2: The atman is eternal and indestructible while the body is mortal — Bhagavad Gita 2:17 states the soul cannot be destroyed. Could also reference Advaita Vedanta teaching that atman and Brahman are ultimately one. Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one textual reference; some development. Developing: Two beliefs stated; one or both underdeveloped or lacking a source. Emerging: One belief with little development.

practice_questions.text:
'It is impossible to worship just one God if you believe in the Hindu Trimurti.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument. Agrees: The Trimurti presents three distinct divine figures with different functions; popular Hinduism includes many deities; Vaishnavism and Shaivism offer different supreme deities. Disagrees: The Trimurti is understood as three aspects of the one Brahman; all deities are ultimately manifestations of the single divine reality; the Bhagavad Gita (7:21) teaches that all devotion ultimately reaches the one God. Non-religious view: a Humanist might argue the multiplicity of deities reflects evolving human attempts to conceptualise the divine rather than evidence of actual theological contradiction. Justified conclusion. Secure: Two developed sides with at least one Hindu source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides, limited evaluation. Emerging: Descriptive, one-sided.

lessons.title: Puja, Pilgrimage and Hindu Rites of Passage

before.content_html:
Puja — Hindu Worship

Puja is the central act of Hindu worship. It involves offering devotion to a deity through ritual actions — presenting flowers, water, food (prasad), light and incense. Puja can take place in the home shrine or in the mandir (temple), and it connects the worshipper directly to the divine. The Bhagavad Gita (3:19) teaches about the importance of acting without attachment to results as a form of duty, and (4:38) speaks of sacred knowledge gained through sincere devotion and practice — foundational principles that underlie Hindu worship.

Key Fact

Daily puja at home is typically performed at a household shrine (puja ghar). The worshipper may wake the deity, bathe and dress the image, offer food, flowers, incense and light a lamp, and recite prayers or mantras. This daily ritual maintains a personal relationship with the divine and structures the Hindu day around devotion.

Congregational Puja in the Mandir

The mandir is the Hindu temple — the earthly home of a deity. At its heart is the murti: the sacred image through which the deity is believed to be present. Hindus do not understand the murti as a mere statue; the image is treated as the living presence of God, cared for, dressed and fed as if alive. This distinction is important — criticisms that Hindus ‘worship idols’ misunderstand the theological basis of murti worship.

Arti is one of the most important acts of congregational puja. A arti lamp with several wicks is lit and waved in a circular motion before the murti, accompanied by bells, singing and the chanting of prayers. The lamp is then offered to the congregation, who cup their hands over the flame and touch their faces — symbolically receiving the deity’s blessing. Arti is typically performed multiple times daily in large temples.

Havan (also called homa) is a sacred fire ceremony performed as part of worship, particularly for significant occasions. Offerings — including grains, ghee (clarified butter) and herbs — are placed into a consecrated fire as the priest chants sacred texts. The fire is considered a messenger between the human and divine realms, carrying offerings upward to the gods.

Bhakti means devotional love — the path of personal, loving devotion to a chosen deity (ishta devata). The bhakti movement, which flourished across India from around the 7th century CE, stressed that liberation (moksha) could be achieved through sincere love for God, not only through ritual or knowledge. Bhakti made Hindu devotion accessible to all, regardless of caste or education.

Bhakti practice takes many forms: singing devotional hymns (bhajan), chanting God’s name (kirtan), performing puja with heartfelt emotion, and reading or hearing the sacred stories of the gods (katha). The Hare Krishna movement (ISKCON) is a well-known modern expression of Vaishnavite bhakti — its members express devotion through chanting the Maha Mantra: ‘Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare’.

Pilgrimage to Varanasi

Varanasi (also known as Benares or Kashi) is one of the most sacred cities in all of Hinduism. Situated on the banks of the River Ganges in northern India, it is believed to be the home of Shiva himself. Pilgrims travel to Varanasi to bathe in the sacred Ganges, which Hindus believe has the power to purify the soul and wash away sins accumulated in past lives. Bathing at the ghats (stone steps leading to the river) is a profoundly important spiritual act.

Dying and being cremated at Varanasi is considered especially auspicious. Hindus believe that those who die there receive liberation (moksha) from the cycle of rebirth directly, because Shiva himself is said to whisper the sacred mantra into the ear of the dying. Varanasi’s famous cremation ghats — in particular the Manikarnika Ghat — burn funeral pyres continuously. For many Hindus, the hope of dying at Varanasi and being cremated there is a lifelong aspiration.

Key Fact

Varanasi is holy because it is believed to be Shiva’s city. Pilgrims bathe in the Ganges to purify the soul. Dying there is believed to grant moksha — liberation from the cycle of rebirth. The Ganges itself is regarded as a goddess and is considered sacred throughout its length.

Hindu Rites of Passage

Hinduism marks the key transitions of life through sacred rites called samskaras. These rites are connected to the broader framework of varnashramadharma — the duties associated with one’s social position and stage of life. The Mahabharata (Book 9.60) references this framework.

Nam Samskar (Naming Ceremony): Shortly after birth, a child is given a name in a formal ceremony. A Hindu priest may cast the child’s horoscope and suggest names beginning with an auspicious letter. The name often reflects one of the divine qualities or names a deity, connecting the child’s identity to the sacred from the very start of life.

Mundane (Head-Shaving Ceremony): In the early years of life, a child’s first hair is shaved. This is seen as removing impurities carried from the previous life. It is understood as a purification rite that prepares the child for the life ahead.

Upanayana (Sacred Thread Ceremony): This initiation rite marks a boy’s transition to student life. A sacred thread is placed across the body, symbolising the second birth into a life of religious learning and duty. Traditionally restricted to the top three varnas, the ceremony involves commitments to study, self-discipline and service to a teacher. After this ceremony, the boy is expected to begin learning the Vedas and other sacred texts.

Hindu marriage (vivah) is one of the most elaborate samskaras. The central ritual involves the couple walking seven times around a sacred fire — these seven steps (saptapadi) represent the couple’s seven vows to each other before God, who is symbolised by the fire. The ceremony is witnessed by the fire as the divine witness, making the marriage a sacred covenant rather than merely a legal contract.

At death, the body is cremated rather than buried. This reflects the Hindu belief that the physical body is temporary — it is the atman (soul) that is eternal and will be reborn. The eldest son plays a crucial role: he lights the funeral pyre and, in traditional practice, may break the skull at the peak of the fire to release the atman from the body. After cremation, the ashes are scattered in a sacred river — ideally the Ganges — completing the soul’s return to the cycle of nature.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Puja — both in the home and in the mandir — is the central act of Hindu devotion. The murti is treated as the living presence of the deity. Arti (light offering) and havan (fire ceremony) are key practices. Bhakti (devotional love) is the spiritual path expressed through puja.
  • Varanasi is Hinduism’s holiest city. Bathing in the Ganges purifies the soul; dying there is believed to grant liberation (moksha) from the cycle of rebirth.
  • Hindu rites of passage (samskaras) mark key life transitions: naming (Nam Samskar), head-shaving (Mundane), sacred thread ceremony (Upanayana), marriage (seven circles around the fire) and cremation (eldest son, ashes scattered in a river).

knowledge_checks.q: What is the 'murti' in a Hindu mandir?
options: The sacred fire used in havan ceremonies
The lamp waved before the deity during arti
The sacred image or statue of a deity, treated as the living presence of God
The priest who leads congregational worship

knowledge_checks.q: Why do Hindus consider dying in Varanasi to be especially auspicious?
options: Because Brahma created the universe there
Because it is believed that Shiva grants liberation (moksha) to those who die there
Because it is the birthplace of Krishna
Because the Bhagavad Gita was written there

knowledge_checks.q: In puja, the _____ lamp is lit and waved before the deity in a circular motion as an act of offering light and devotion.
The Hindu sacred thread ceremony, which marks a boy's 'second birth' into a life of religious learning, is called _____.
Match each Hindu rite of passage to its purpose:
right: Naming a child; connecting identity to the sacred from birth
Sacred thread ceremony; marks transition to religious student life
Releases the atman from the body; ashes scattered in a sacred river

before.exam_tip_html: When writing about Hindu worship or rites of passage, avoid describing what happens without explaining the religious meaning. For example, don’t just say ‘the arti lamp is waved before the deity’ — explain that the light symbolises the offering of devotion and the receiving of the deity’s blessing. Similarly, for the sacred thread ceremony, explain the significance of ‘second birth’ rather than just listing the features. Examiners reward the ‘why’ as well as the ‘what’.

lessons.title: Karma, Reincarnation, Varna and Hindu Festivals

before.content_html:
Karma and Samsara

Karma means ‘action’ in Sanskrit. In Hinduism, it refers to the moral law of cause and effect: every intentional action — physical, verbal or mental — generates consequences that shape the soul’s future existence. Good actions generate positive karma, leading towards better future lives and ultimately liberation. Bad actions generate negative karma, leading to suffering and lower rebirths. The Bhagavad Gita (2:13) describes how the soul passes from one body to the next just as a person moves from childhood to youth to old age — the soul continuing through a long chain of lives.

Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth within which all living beings are caught. The Bhagavad Gita (2:13, 2:15, 2:22) develops this teaching: just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on others that are new, so the soul casts off worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. Samsara is not a punishment in itself — it is the ongoing process of the soul’s journey — but it involves suffering because of attachment to the material world. The ultimate goal is to escape samsara entirely.

Key Fact

Karma is the law of moral cause and effect. Samsara is the cycle of rebirth it drives. Moksha is liberation from samsara — the soul’s reunion with Brahman, the ultimate reality. These three concepts form the backbone of the Hindu understanding of the soul’s journey.

Varnashramadharma — The Four Varnas

Hindu society has traditionally been organised according to the concept of varna (often translated as caste). The four varnas are: Brahmin (priests and teachers), Kshatriya (warriors and rulers), Vaishya (merchants and farmers) and Shudra (labourers and servants). Beyond the four varnas are the Dalits (historically called ‘untouchables’), who were placed outside the varna system entirely and assigned the most polluting tasks.

Within each varna are many jatis — hereditary occupational sub-groups. The varna and jati system has had a profound impact on social life in South Asia: determining marriage partners, occupation, diet and social interaction. The status of Dalits was, for centuries, one of severe marginalisation and discrimination. Today, the Dalit community has fought for and won legal protections — the Indian constitution outlaws caste discrimination — but social prejudice can persist. In Hindu communities in the UK, varna distinctions are generally less rigidly observed than in parts of South Asia, though they still influence marriage patterns.

Several modern movements within Hinduism have challenged traditional caste hierarchies. ISKCON (the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, known as the Hare Krishna movement) teaches that all people, regardless of birth, can achieve devotion to Krishna and spiritual advancement. ISKCON accepts members of all backgrounds and nationalities, directly challenging the idea that caste is spiritually determining.

The Ramakrishna Mission, founded in the late 19th century by Swami Vivekananda, emphasised the unity of all people and the equality of all paths to God. Vivekananda taught that service to humanity was service to God (daridra narayan — God in the poor), directly challenging the view that Dalits were spiritually inferior. Both movements reflect an ongoing internal reform process within Hinduism.

The Four Ashramas

Alongside the varna system, Hinduism describes four stages of life (ashramas). The first is brahmacharya (student life) — dedicated to learning, celibacy and service to the teacher. The second is grihastha (householder) — marriage, raising children, professional work and maintaining the home. The third is vanaprastha (forest-dweller or retirement) — withdrawing from worldly duties to focus on spiritual practice. The fourth is sannyasa (renunciant) — the final stage of complete renunciation, with no home or possessions, focused solely on liberation. The ideal Hindu life moves through all four ashramas, each with its appropriate duties (dharma).

Hindu Festivals

Diwali (also spelled Divali) is often called the Festival of Lights. It is celebrated across South Asia and in Hindu communities worldwide, and lasts five days. For Vaishnavas (devotees of Vishnu), Diwali is associated particularly with the return of Rama and Sita to Ayodhya after their fourteen-year exile and Rama’s defeat of the demon king Ravana — the story told in the Ramayana. Lamps and fireworks celebrate this homecoming. For Shaktas (devotees of the goddess), Diwali is associated with the goddess Lakshmi (goddess of wealth and prosperity), who is believed to visit clean, well-lit homes. Rangoli patterns, diyas (oil lamps), fireworks and gift-giving are central practices.

Holi is a joyful spring festival, celebrated with coloured powders, water and dancing. Its origins lie in two stories. The first is the story of Holika and Prahlada: Holika was a demoness who tried to kill the young devotee Prahlada (a devoted worshipper of Vishnu), but she was destroyed while Prahlada survived, demonstrating that devotion to God protects the righteous. A bonfire (Holika dahan) the night before the main celebration remembers her destruction. The second story celebrates the divine love of Krishna and Radha — Krishna is associated with colour and playfulness, and the throwing of coloured powder is connected to his relationship with Radha and the gopis (cowgirls) of Vrindavan.

Ahimsa means non-violence or non-harm. It is one of Hinduism’s most important ethical principles, flowing from the belief that all living beings contain the atman — the divine soul. To harm any living creature is, in this sense, to harm God. Ahimsa is expressed practically through vegetarianism, which is widely practised among Hindus, particularly Brahmins and Vaishnavas. The Hare Krishna movement’s Food for Life programme distributes free vegetarian meals to those in need — embodying both ahimsa and the duty of social service.

Environmental concern also flows from ahimsa. The Chipko movement (‘tree-huggers’) began in the 1970s in northern India as villagers, many of them women, embraced trees to prevent loggers from cutting them down. Drawing on Hindu reverence for nature and the principle of ahimsa towards all life, the movement became an influential early example of environmental activism. The sacred forest at Vrindavan (associated with Krishna’s childhood) has been the subject of conservation efforts by Hindu communities who regard it as sacred land.

Key Fact

Holi has two origin stories: Holika and Prahlada (devotion to Vishnu conquers evil) and Krishna and Radha (divine love and playfulness). Diwali celebrates Rama and Sita’s return (Vaishnavas) or honours Lakshmi (Shaktas). Both festivals are celebrated with light, colour and community.
before.exam_tip_html: Questions about karma often invite students to explain both the concept and its implications for how Hindus live. Don’t just define karma — explain that it motivates ethical behaviour (every action has consequences), supports the practice of ahimsa (harming others generates bad karma), and gives meaning to the varna system (one’s birth reflects past-life karma). For festival questions, name the story, explain what it celebrates and describe two or three actual practices — examiners are looking for both knowledge of content and understanding of significance.
